newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Good year for oil trade, courtesy of Saddam.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Good year for oil trade, courtesy of Saddam.

text.p: Oil trading companies are enjoying one of their best years in a decade thanks to the unlikely combination of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and low oil storage tanks.

After a miserable 1995, prices this year have yo-yoed on a drip-feed of developments in the Iraqi oil-for-food saga, a U.N. deal which may eventually allow Baghdad to resume crude oil exports for the first time since the Gulf War.
Jitters have been exacerbated by an oil company drive to reduce costs by running on minimum stocks, leaving buyers more vulnerable to supply shortages.
But despite better profits top oil traders are in cautious mood. The oil market often has a sting in its tail and trading conditions can change as quickly as prices.

"This year has been good for trading, but for specific reasons. Low stocks have encouraged volatility and Iraq has kept people guessing all year," said Bob Finch, head of trading in London at Vitol SA, one of the world's largest traders.

Saddam's latest military adventure into Kurdish safe havens last weekend injected another dose of the jitters into the market and drove Brent crude oil to a post-Gulf War high of $23.50 a barrel. Price volatility in Brent has averaged nearly 38 percent so far this year compared to 20 percent in 1995.
But sharp price moves alone are not enough to ensure better market conditions.
"Short term volatility tends to reflect outside political events rather than the underlying health or liquidity of the market," said Finch.
The oil price crash of 1986 and the Gulf War in 1991 were tough for the oil market and the fallout was damaging.
"The impact of those events took several years. Some of the smaller trading companies were shaken out which has inevitably hit liquidity in recent years," Finch said.
Some 20 to 30 oil trading companies have gone to the wall since the champagne days of the 1980s but the outlook is better now than for several years.
The large multi-national oil companies such as Shell, British Petroleum and Exxon have a strong interest in the long-term health of the oil markets.
John Gabriel, general manager of crude trading co-ordination at Shell's international trading company STASCO sees the market recovery being helped by its ability to change quickly.
"Its adaptability makes it robust and should enable it to recover from shocks and take opportunities quickly," he said.
"You have to be cautious but those companies that have remained in the market tend to have the skills and financial resources to stay the course."
Despite growing market savvy among big banks and oil companies the room for agile and flexible trading companies may grow over the next few years.
In particular, the deregulation of oil markets in Asia, Latin America, Africa and eastern Europe promises new trading opportunities.
Also, the new trend for major oil companies to work with minimum oil stocks lends itself to higher volatility which should encourage trading opportunities.

Earlier this year the price of oil for prompt delivery soared compared to the price of forward oil traded on futures and derivatives markets. This huge backwardation was created and sustained because oil buyers had very little oil in their tanks.
Many oil buyers got caught in a honey trap this year by using up their oil stocks early in the year, hoping that prices would fall when Iraq resumed oil exports.
But Iraq's oil-for-food deal has been put on ice after Saddam's weekend foray into Kurdistan leaving some buyers dangerously low on stocks.

Some will have little choice but to pay huge premiums for prompt oil. "Having reduced stocks it is very expensive for buyers to re-fill tanks when the backwardation is so big," said Arie Silverberg at Glencore UK Ltd in London.
